item.title: Cowboys legend Randy White endorses Ken Paxton, warns James Talarico ‘can’t be trusted’
item.description: Dallas Cowboys legend Randy White endorsed Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race, citing concerns over transgender athletes in girls' sports and bathrooms.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Dallas Cowboys legend and Pro Football Hall of Famer Randy White has endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in the state’s consequential U.S. Senate race.

"Ken Paxton will get in there and get things done. He’s not afraid," White told OutKick in an exclusive interview. "That’s one thing I really like about Ken. He will get in there and say what needs to be said. He doesn’t hold back. He tells the truth. He’s not trying to win a popularity contest when he’s working. It’s what’s right for the people."

White said his endorsement grew out of his personal relationship with Paxton and their shared work on issues involving children and the opioid crisis.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"I got to know Ken as a person, and I think he is a super person," White said. "I like his attitude, the things that he does, the way he does them."

White highlighted Paxton’s support for the National Child Identification Program, which provides parents with kits to preserve their children’s fingerprints, DNA and other identifying information at home. Paxton previously joined a coalition supporting federal funding for the program, while White has served as one of its Hall of Fame ambassadors.

"He is a big supporter of the Child ID program, which is something I’m a big supporter of — helping kids," White said.

White also lost his son-in-law to an accidental opioid overdose, a personal tragedy that prompted him to become an advocate for drug-awareness initiatives. In 2024, White joined Paxton and Texas parents who had lost children to fentanyl-laced drugs in a public service announcement released by the attorney general’s office.

EXCLUSIVE: FENTANYL DEATHS PLUNGE 22% AS TRUMP WHITE HOUSE TOUTS CRACKDOWN ON DEADLY DRUG CRISIS

"This opioid stuff — I lost a son-in-law to opioids, accidental," White said. "He’s been right on top of that ever since that happened. Everything he does is kind of the way I think it should be done."

TALARICO SAYS HE 'MISSED THE MARK' AS HE BACKTRACKS ON CONTROVERSIAL WOKE STATEMENTS

White drew a stark contrast between Paxton and Talarico, whom he said he does not trust.

"I know Ken Paxton," White said. "I know he’s going to do what he says he’s going to do. I know he’s going to go to work every day, and he’s going to help the people of Texas. This other guy, I don’t know him. But I hear what he says, and it’s different from what I believe."

Asked whether he considered Talarico "too woke," White answered, "Yes."

"I don’t want to go into each specific thing, but, yeah, he’s different than what I think is right," White said. "If this guy gets elected in Texas, I’m going to pull my hair out, and I don’t have many left. So, we’ve got to get out and vote so this doesn’t happen."

White specifically cited transgender participation in girls’ sports and access to girls’ bathrooms among the issues on which he disagreed with Democrats and Talarico.

Talarico voted against Republican-backed restrictions on transgender athletes while serving in the Texas House. In September, however, he told Fox News that he would "oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it risks safety or fairness."

Talarico later said his position had not changed, arguing that he opposes a blanket statewide prohibition and believes local education and sports officials should make decisions on an athlete-by-athlete and sport-by-sport basis.

White said Talarico’s recent comments reinforced his doubts about the Democrat.

"I think that’s a sign that we can’t trust him," White said. "He’s going to go with the way the wind flows, whatever he feels like is the best thing for him and what his goals are. We don’t need somebody like that.

"We need somebody like Ken Paxton who is going to stick to his guns, who is not afraid to stand up for what he believes is right."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Talarico's office has not responded to a request for comment.

Paxton secured the Republican nomination in May after defeating longtime Sen. John Cornyn in a primary runoff, an outcome that underscored President Donald Trump’s influence over the Republican Party. Trump endorsed Paxton shortly before the runoff.

The general-election race has become unexpectedly competitive. A Fox News Poll conducted Sept. 24-28 found Talarico leading Paxton 51%-49% among likely voters, a result within the poll’s three-point margin of sampling error. Several other recent public polls have also shown Talarico narrowly ahead.

White nevertheless expressed unequivocal support for Trump, whose political standing and handling of the economy have become central issues in the race.

"I love President Trump. I’m behind him 1,000%," White said. "These gas prices, we’re paying a little more for gas right now. But I tell you what, he’s saving the world. And we’ve got to pay a little bit more for gas — OK, well, let’s pay it for a while.

"He’ll get gas prices back down where they were. It’s just something that’s part of the process of getting America back where it needs to be and making it safe."

White also backed Trump’s handling of the war with Iran.

"We had to do it. You had to," White said. "They’re never going to stop. They are never going to stop. … What President Trump is doing, I think, is the best thing for our country."

item.title: Fever star Sophie Cunningham tells Aces' A'ja Wilson to 'grow up' in response to her playoff meltdown
item.description: Sophie Cunningham blasted A'ja Wilson on her "No Hesitation" podcast for confronting a Fever fan who was simply pointing during the WNBA playoffs.
item.content:encoded:
If you know anything about Indiana Fever forward Sophie Cunningham, you know she's not going to mince words. She famously stated, "I said what I said," while speaking to the media following relentless backlash for saying men should not compete in women's sports. 

That’s why it shouldn’t shock anyone that Cunningham went off on WNBA MVP and Las Vegas Aces star A’ja Wilson for confronting a Fever fan and verbally berating him in Game 2 at Gainbridge Fieldhouse for simply pointing at her.

In the latest episode of "No Hesitation," hosted by Cunningham and elite basketball trainer Drew Hanlen, the Fever forward gave her long-awaited take on the now-infamous incident involving the controversial blocking call.

"Oh my God! I have so many thoughts," Cunningham stated after her and Hanlen watched a clip from the "Pat McAfee Show" where one of the hosts (Boston Connor) confirmed, just as I did in my reporting following the incident, that the fan said, "It (the foul) is on you," while pointing.

CRAIG CARTON BLASTS WNBA, A'JA WILSON OVER FAN CONFRONTATION: 'THIS LEAGUE CAN'T GET OUT OF ITS OWN WAY'

While explaining that she held back from giving her reaction to the incident on X and saving it "for the pod," Cunningham went off on Wilson. "Us women in sport, and I'm just gonna say women in sport because that's my occupation and I have lived this, we yell from the rooftops that we want equality. We want to be treated like the men," she stated, prefacing her blunt comments.

"We're gonna go for them for just pointing and saying, 'You fouled!'? Like grow up! What are we doing?" Cunningham said.

She also took exception to the idea that Wilson, and seemingly other players, should be allowed to attack fans, claiming, "Us athletes need to be treated better" and "These fans need to be more supportive and not say anything negative."

Cunningham pointed out that she has a unique perspective on this as one of the most, if not the most, hated WNBA players simply because she doesn’t believe men should be in women's sports and spaces. "I can say this, because I, hands down, have probably got s--- on the entire season, maybe sometimes two seasons — people coming after who I am, my character, what I stand for, x, y, z, I could go on and on."

WHO IS SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM? FOX NATION CHRONICLES THE WNBA STAR'S RISE FROM FARM GIRL TO WOMEN'S SPORTS ADVOCATE

"I've heard the worst of the worst. It's part of it," Cunningham said.

"You should be grateful to be on this platform. You should be grateful to be playing basketball for a living and inspiring the next generation. If you really want sports fans, then you're gonna get sports fans. That includes pointing. That includes getting yelled at. Probably [will] be getting called names."

"I don't think [the Fever fan] did absolutely anything wrong," Cunningham said definitively.

Maybe Cunningham's most controversial take was saying, "If you want to get technical, that (Wilson's actions) could've called for a suspension, but she's like the LeBron James of our league so of course they're (WNBA) not going to suspend her." 

Not only was Wilson not suspended, she was neither ejected, nor was she fined for her actions. Cunningham seems to say players of Wilson's caliber will be treated far less harshly and get away with clear violations.

Cunningham also said there should have been repercussions for former Fever guard and Amazon Prime commentator Sydney Colson, as well as fellow Amazon analyst Theresa Plaisance, who left their courtside seats to insert themselves in the altercation.

"There's definitely a double standard," Cunningham stated.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

As for her feelings about whether her and her team wanted Wilson to play, while waiting for the league to announce if they would punish the Aces' star, Cunningham cleared the air saying, "We wanted her to play. I think that makes for good basketball."

"Who would've thought that someone pointing would cause so many people to go into a mental spiral? That says a lot more about your mental status to anything the fans are doing," Cunningham said in response to both Wilson and viewers upset over her poking fun at the situation on TikTok.

Cunningham and her co-host also spent a few minutes comparing the Game 2 incident involving Wilson and the fan with an Aces fan who stepped onto the court and pointed at Lexie Hull following a controversial foul call in Game 3.

Here's how fans, media and others reacted in the replies on X to Cunningham's comments:

Cunningham continues to be a refreshing addition to the player-led commentary space. She tells it like it is, without apology. We need more athletes like her. While her teammate Raven Johnson apologized to A’ja Wilson on Friday via X for comments perceived as insensitive during a media appearance with Myisha Hines-Allen about Hines-Allen’s altercation and hard foul on Wilson, Cunningham stands firm in her beliefs and feels no need to bow to the WNBA establishment, which includes Wilson.

item.title: Jon Gruden fires up Trump rally crowd in Ohio as if delivering a locker room speech then delivers endorsement
item.description: Jon Gruden took the stage at Trump's Ohio rally to endorse former University of Dayton teammate Jon Husted, urging the crowd to vote early Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
Super Bowl winning football coach Jon Gruden had an NFL reputation for using his fire and enthusiasm, not to mention his offensive strategies, to great success and we saw some of that at the rally President Donald Trump held Saturday night in Ohio.

First of all, who knew Gruden was a conservative?

He watched the president deliver his message standing side-by-side with Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, who is running for re-election, and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

And at one point during Trump's comments, a protester began to say something or other, and was escorted out while the crowd chanted, "Na Na Hey Hey Kiss Him Goodbye."

"You know, Jon Gruden is standing here, saying, 'I don't believe this. This is rougher than a football game,'" Trump told the crowd. "There's more spirit. I think they have more spirit here than they did today in Ohio State, if you want to know the truth."

Gruden, who coached the Tampa Bay Buccaneers to a Super Bowl title and later coached the Raiders in both Oakland and Las Vegas for 53 games before resigning in 2021, was introduced to the crowd by Husted.

Husted and Gruden were teammates on the 1985 University of Dayton football team and have remained close through the years.

"I'll be very brief, but I want to thank everybody for showing up," Gruden told the crowd that greeted him with applause. "I love you guys. I just came back for one reason and I'm from Ohio. My mom and dad are from Cleveland. I was born in Sandusky and I went to the University of Dayton.

"And I'm damn proud of it, man!"

Yes, the crowd loved that and the cheers were evidence of that.

Then came the endorsement of his former teammate and friend:

"Jon Husted is a lot more than my friend," Gruden said. "He was a great player." He intercepted 17 passes on the gridiron. He was a great player. And I know why he's a great player. It was because of his work ethic and his commitment and his day-to-day mental toughness."

Husted, who has served as an Ohio state representative, Ohio House speaker, state senator, secretary of state, lieutenant governor and, since January 2025, a U.S. senator, was an All-American cornerback and kick returner at Dayton.

FROM LOCKER ROOMS TO CONGRESS: JAY FEELY LATEST ATHLETE SEEKING TO TAKE LESSONS IN LEADERSHIP TO CAPITOL HILL

He was a starter on the Flyers’ 1989 NCAA Division III national championship team. Dayton finished that season 13-0-1, and Husted recorded an interception in the championship-game victory over Union.

"He will never quit, ever on you or anybody," Gruden bellowed. "Let's hear it, for Husted. Right. I'm gonna close with this ... Before you know it, last thing I'm gonna say, before you know it, this election is over, yes? It's over.

"But what we got to do is we got to do our part. Early voting starts Tuesday. Can we be there or not? Let's be there! And I know you guys got a lot more friends than I do. Get your friends, and get their friends and their friends, and let's get Husted back in action. Let's go!"

item.title: More Gen Z college freshmen are quitting school early and moving back home with mom and dad
item.description: Just weeks into the fall semester, some Gen Z college freshmen have left campus and headed back home to take online classes — creating viral debates about the reasons.
item.content:encoded:
Some Gen Z freshmen have already decided — just weeks into the fall semester — to abandon their college campuses, head back home and take classes online.

Others are quitting school entirely very early on.

In a recent "Outnumbered" segment, the Fox News co-hosts discussed the trend of young college students bailing out of campus life and returning home — saying the degree is what they’re after, not the "college experience."

Online reactions to the controversial and trending decision are running the gamut. 

‘SHUT UP’ AND LISTEN: TRACE GALLAGHER SHARES WISDOM LEARNED FROM BEING A ‘GIRL DAD’

"To be fair, college is not for everyone," one Facebook user commented.

Another blurted, "Time for the school of HARD KNOCKS!"

A viral TikTok posted by a 17-year-old indicated that the student left campus at Southern University in Louisiana just two weeks into her first semester to go back home to Las Vegas, according to reports. 

Some students today seem to be strangers with discomfort and struggle — as one user advised, "Y'all have to learn how to be uncomfortable."

Another was more understanding, posting, "It's OK to be uncomfortable, anxious and stressed during your first year of college."

"Outnumbered" co-host Kaleigh McEnany said she remembered her own college days, when she would struggle to return to school after spending time at home.

"I would cry in the airport, and my mom was like, 'You've gotta get on the plane, you've gotta go back …' And it was tough, but I'm so glad she pushed me," she said.

In her viral TikTok, the teenager shared a disclaimer in the caption of her video, noting that she didn’t drop out — she switched to the school’s online program instead.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Various factors affect the decisions of students to leave campus and take classes at home — with some online posters on various forums weighing in with their own experiences and beliefs. 

Writing on Reddit recently, one parent said a son in the family's household "is quitting college quickly, and I feel like a loser."

The parent went on, "He was one of the top students in his high school class. Had anxiety, but worked through all issues eventually. I have anxiety issues as well, so I've always done my best to help him through it. Dished out so much money to get him a car, a laptop, paid for bus passes, etc., only to have him drop out after one week."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The person continued, "Won't even consider just sticking with it for a semester or two. He even had a scholarship to cover his entire first year! I mean, I took 19 years to finish my bachelor's degree, but I was always employed, so what can I really say?"

In response, another person on Reddit wrote, "What are his reasons? How much ability do you have to force him to stay? Is it a done deal already? I would absolutely try to get to the bottom of it and figure out how to work around whatever his concerns are."

Another parent weighed in with this experience: "My daughter has a lot of social anxiety and just got through her second week of college. She is particularly anxious about public speaking. So much so she would miss days of high school almost any time it was required. I have been very nervous about her ability to adapt."

Added the parent, "So far it is going well, but not without some struggle. One of her classes required discussion from everyone, each time."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Still another individual shared a very different perspective.

"I feel that college is a huge maturity checkpoint and most young adults aren't ready for it right out of high school," the person wrote.

"I am a big proponent of not pushing them toward it until they feel it's something they want to do. That doesn't mean there aren't expectations — but maybe there is an option to choose to work full time, and pay some bills instead."

Others chimed in on that same theme.

"There is NO reason he has to attend college right now. He can work and see whether he is able to earn enough to support himself that way. He may need a break from academics. There are many paths; don't stress!"

Students and online commenters have pointed out that financial concerns, mental health struggles or the desire to simply focus on academics can make on-campus life more difficult for some young people.

The "Outnumbered" segment also noted that many members of Gen Z completed high school largely from home — taking online classes in their living room or kitchen, with parents not far away, during the COVID pandemic. 

A recent Psychology Today piece on the topic noted that kids who leave college early — for whatever reason — need clear guidance once they get back home. 

"Set clear boundaries regarding work, household responsibilities, health and wellness, and daily routines," a mental health counselor advised parents.

item.title: Dems hand GOP fresh midterm weapon by opposing widely used voter ID
item.description: Senate Democrats blocked a voter ID and insider trading ban bill as Republicans like Chuck Schumer's caucus face accusations of denying Trump a win.
item.content:encoded:
Senate Democrats’ recent rejection of voter ID is giving Republicans fresh ammunition in the midterm fight, putting them on the opposite side of a practice that is common across the country and broadly popular with voters in both parties.

Republicans have developed a cynical view of why Democrats won’t play ball with voter ID, arguing that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and his caucus don’t want to give the GOP a win heading into the midterm elections.

"Democrats are gonna vote against it because they don't want to give the president a win," Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital. "They don’t want to give Republicans a win. They'll screw the country and stuff."

DOZENS OF HOUSE DEMOCRATS REJECT BILL FUSING CONGRESSIONAL STOCK BAN WITH FEDERAL VOTER ID

Republicans' latest attempt to pass a federal voter ID law, which was paired with another popular issue to ban insider trading in Congress, comes months after initially launching their push to pass the SAVE America Act, a high priority for President Donald Trump that Schumer and Democrats have time and again rejected.

Earlier this year, Democrats argued that voter ID isn’t so bad, it’s just how Republicans were approaching it that they disagreed with — Schumer dubbed the SAVE America Act "Jim Crow 2.0" and contended it would disenfranchise Black and Brown voters.

"Democrats support voter ID," Schumer said on a press call earlier this year. "In fact, we included it, and it is included, in our Freedom to Vote legislation several years ago."

INSIDE THE SENATE'S CHAOTIC ALL-NIGHTER THAT LEFT TRUMP'S SAVE AMERICA ACT ON THE SHELF

But as the months have dragged on, an issue that voters overwhelmingly support has become a place for Democrats to dig their heels into the dirt against.

Requiring identification to vote is already a practice in 36 states. Of those, 23 require photo ID, while 13 accept another form of identification, such as a bank statement. Nine of those states have Democratic senators.

"We already have it," Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told Fox News Digital. "I mean, Virginia has a voter ID law that our citizens really like."

"Virtually every state has a voter ID law," he continued. "So, what, there has to be a one size fits all federal thing for states [that[ are already doing this?"

SCHUMER, DEMOCRATS SAY THEY SUPPORT VOTER ID, THEN BLOCK GOP AMENDMENT TO REQUIRE IT

Republicans say that the Democratic resistance has a more nefarious intent. Requiring voter ID would allegedly nuke some of their voter base, illegal immigrants, and therefore lower their chances of winning in federal elections.

"Well, it's evident Democrats want to make it easier to cheat," Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., told Fox News Digital. " Republicans want to make it easier to vote, make sure nobody's cheating. And that's where we are on this voter ID, an 80/20 issue or not even more."

Barrasso argued that identification is required in several mundane instances of life, from boarding a plane to buying a beer — and even to get into some rallies held by Democratic candidates during this election cycle.

"They’re complete hypocrites on this," Barrasso said. "But [what] we need to do is elect more Republicans to be able to win these elections and make sure we have people here that see what the American people see, which is, you have to have a photo ID to vote."

item.title: Robert Blake’s son returns to restaurant tied to family tragedy for new murder mystery
item.description: Noah Blake opens "A Killer Night in Studio City" at Vitello's, confronting decades of pain tied to his father Robert Blake's infamous trial.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-five years after Vitello's became part of a painful chapter in his family's history, Noah Blake has returned to the restaurant to direct and star in a fictional murder mystery, describing the production as part of his healing journey.

The "Teen Witch" alum's "A Killer Night in Studio City," a noir-inspired immersive theater production set in 1958, opened at the famed Italian restaurant on Sept. 15.

"When I was first approached about this, of course, there was this little bit of ... and then I was like, 'Wait, what am I doing? Of course, I should do this,'" Blake told Fox News Digital. "This is a chance for me to, not rewrite history, but to create a new page and to create a new connection and a new relationship for me with this place, for my name with this place, for my family with this place."

ROBERT BLAKE DEAD AT 89

"I've got a four-year-old son," Blake said. "I want him to be able to go there and enjoy Vitello's as he's grown up, God willing, as long as Vitello's is there. And I don't want him to ever feel funny. I want him to think about, 'Oh, Vitello's, that's the place where daddy did that fun show.' Not this other stuff. I'm not trying to minimize that tragedy, but it wasn't my tragedy, and it was a cross that I've had to bear and still will probably for the rest of my life."

Blake said Vitello's was a regular gathering place for his family while he was growing up, but he stayed away for decades. He eventually returned and agreed to stage the production there, saying he wanted to reclaim positive memories of a place he had loved.

"I want to go and do something in this space that is creative, that is fun, that is exciting, where people come and laugh and gasp and have a great time," he explained. "Some people may not even know [what happened] and the people who do might be curious and go, 'Oh, that has nothing to do with anything, and I had a great time.'"

WATCH: NOAH BLAKE SAYS RETURN TO SITE TIED TO FAMILY TRAGEDY IS ‘FULL CIRCLE’

The history Blake is trying to move beyond dates back to 2001, when his father Robert Blake's wife, Bonny Lee Bakley, was killed after the couple had dinner at Vitello's.

The actor was acquitted of murder in 2005 in connection with Bakley's killing. Bakley was shot and killed while sitting in Robert's car near the restaurant. A civil jury later found him liable for her death and ordered him to pay Bakley's family $30 million, prompting him to file for bankruptcy, according to The Associated Press.

An appeals court later reduced the award to $15 million, after which the parties reached a confidential settlement. Robert died in 2023 at 89.

Rose Lenore, Bakley's daughter with Robert, feels differently about the production. She told Fox News Digital that Vitello's remains too painful for her and others who loved her mother.

"I think him doing it at Vitello's is upsetting for me and anyone who loved Bonny," she said. "And there were quite a few people who did. She left behind three children, plus me. She also left behind a sister, my aunt, who misses her dearly. And so, to have Robert Blake's son do any show at Vitello's, let alone a murder mystery show, I find that to be insensitive and upsetting."

"I don't even care what the show is about," Lenore said. "I'm also not here to invalidate anyone's healing journey, if that's what this is for him. But I also think it's my moral obligation to stand up for what I believe in. I would still be upset if he was doing anything else. And for Noah to be doing a happy, fun show — I think it's in poor taste."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"I'm not wishing any harm on Noah," Lenore continued. "I wish him well in his life and career. But it would be hard for me to stay silent on something like this. It would be hard for me to stay silent about my mother."

Responding to Lenore's criticism, Blake wrote in a statement to Fox News Digital, "I have my own deeply personal reasons for doing this play. Vitello's was a place that I loved my entire life. Over time, that place became the physical embodiment for me of a much larger and devastating chapter of my life — one thing that I had nothing to do with, but whose consequences I have had to endure for years."

"Choosing to walk back into that space now and create something uniquely mine — something lighthearted and entertaining that people are enjoying — is part of my own healing journey," he wrote. "It's about taking a place that had come to represent something painfully dark in my life and allowing it to represent something else. I'm not erasing history or rewriting it. I'm simply adding a new page to it, and I don't ask or expect anyone else to sign off on what I need to do to heal."

"Rose is absolutely entitled to her feelings," Blake continued. "I've been there for her many times over the years, and I care for her. She chose to express her feelings about this publicly, which certainly wouldn't have been my choice and still isn't. I would much rather have had a private conversation with her. I've reached out and asked her to call me so that we could talk about this, and that conversation has yet to happen. But that door remains open for her."

Blake said returning to Vitello's has also forced him to revisit his complicated relationship with his late father.

"I don't think people really realize when something like that happens, how many lives are impacted in such a profound way," he explained. "I had to wrestle with who my father really was for everything I thought he was or knew or saw him as. Did he do this thing? Was he really capable of this? Was he that far gone? Was my father this monster?"

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"It's tough because it makes you question a lot. 'What is my genetic makeup?' It was years of intense scrutiny, and it was impossible to live my life, and for other people as well. It's not cool to know that this guy's son had a nervous breakdown and couldn't leave his house for six months and was having panic attacks and night sweats and was incapable of functioning."

"There were moments my father could be a very loving, kind, decent, generous human being," he said. "And there were times when he could just be an absolute f---ing monster and just the worst kind of selfish and menacing and threatening."

Before his death, Robert fiercely denied murdering Bakley.

For Blake, returning to the restaurant carries a meaning beyond the fictional story he says he wants to tell. While he recognizes the connection others may make to his family's past, Blake stressed he does not want that history to define him.

"... I live my life as me," he said.

item.title: DR MARC SIEGEL: The angels behind Alcoholics Anonymous still inspire hope
item.description: Middle-aged adults are drinking more and dying at alarming rates from alcohol use disorder, but a faith-based cure from the 1930s still works.
item.content:encoded:
Alcohol is still something to be worried about. Granted, national data shows a decline coming out of the pandemic, but the overall numbers are still higher than they were in 2018. Not only that, but though Gen Zers and millennials are drinking less, middle-aged adults are drinking more, with an increase in heavy drinking since 2018.

Some of this is because middle-aged adults face increased pressures as they try to manage both aging parents and children who are in adolescence or early adulthood and are just finding themselves. But though drinking may temporarily ease stress, the long-term health risks are significant. A recent study from Colorado determined that older adults are more likely to drink alone, which carries with it additional health risks, including cognitive decline.

There are an estimated 28 million Americans who suffer from alcohol use disorder, with a substantial portion of them being middle-aged. Not only that, but about 50% of the deaths due to alcohol in the U.S. occur among middle-aged adults.

HEAVY DRINKING SURGES AMONG AMERICANS IN ONE AGE GROUP AS OTHER GENERATIONS CUT BACK

Faith-based cures remain highly effective for alcoholism, with none more effective than Alcoholics Anonymous, which was developed in the 1930s by Bill Wilson and Dr. Bob Smith after a chance meeting, the kind that the famed psychiatrist Carl Jung called synchronicity, or meaningful coincidence. 

They became messengers of God for each other and ultimately, for millions of other alcoholics with their 12-step program based largely on making a spiritual connection.

In my new book, "The Angels Among Us," I devote a chapter to the miracle recovery of Bill Wilson and his consequential friendship with Dr. Bob. Bill is admitted to Towns Hospital in New York City in 1934 for the fourth time because of alcohol intoxication followed by withdrawal. He is in the depths of despair and is not sure if he will survive. And then he experiences the central miracle of his life as he demands that God show Himself.

CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND

"The room lights up with a blinding glare of light. Wilson is seized by an ecstasy he has never known. He stands on a mountaintop with a great wind blowing. He thinks to himself, 'This is not a wind of air. This is spirit. This is the God of the preachers.'

"Bill feels that a great, clean strength is blowing through him, that he is now free."

Bill Wilson tells about his experience to his medical angel, Dr. Silkworth, who is tending to him there in the hospital, who decides he is not crazy, but that a great psychic event has occurred. This changes Bill's life, as the doctor/"angel" advises him to hang on to this experience and to share it.

item.title: 10-minute fitness habit can help adults over 40 maintain muscle and stay strong
item.description: CEO Carl Daikeler compares metabolism to a furnace: Muscle is the coal and cardio stokes it, urging a balance of strength training and cardiovascular work.
item.content:encoded:
Adults over 40 may not need to spend hours in the gym to maintain muscle, preserve mobility and stay strong.

According to Los Angeles fitness entrepreneur Carl Daikeler, just 10 minutes of targeted resistance exercise each day can help preserve muscle, mobility and long-term function.

Daikeler, 63, who has spent 28 years leading BODi, the fitness brand formerly known as Beachbody, says his approach to exercise stems from a practical desire to stay healthy without having to be a dedicated fitness enthusiast.

4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS

"I don't like to eat healthy, I don't like to work out," Daikeler told Fox News Digital at the Strong New York conference in September. "I'm just constantly trying to figure out how I can hack my way without having to overturn my life to become one of these diehard health and fitness people, because I'm never going to become that."

For adults looking to stay healthy in midlife, Daikeler recommends what he considers a "minimum effective dose" — short, targeted resistance workouts at home instead of lengthy gym sessions.

"Ten minutes a day, and you can establish and build and maintain muscle," he said.

WANT TO AGE BETTER? RESEARCHERS SAY 4-MINUTE ROUTINE MAY HELP PREVENT DANGEROUS FALLS

Federal physical activity guidelines say that adults should perform muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups at least two days per week, in addition to regular aerobic activity.

Rather than doing a full-body workout every day, Daikeler recommends rotating muscle groups — focusing on the chest one day, upper body the next, then legs and glutes — to build consistency without requiring lengthy gym sessions.

"Do that consistently, and you're going to find your strength return, your muscles return, your joints will start to respond appropriately," he said.

The 10-minute approach can be especially valuable for people taking GLP-1 medications, who may be trying to preserve muscle mass and bone density while losing weight but may feel intimidated by traditional gyms, Daikeler said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

For individuals seeking more significant weight loss, he recommends extending daily activity to 20 or 30 minutes, incorporating a balance of strength training and cardiovascular exercise.

Daikeler cautioned against focusing exclusively on either cardio or resistance training, noting that different exercise types serve distinct functions in the body.

"Your body's like a furnace," Daikeler said. "The coal in that furnace is muscle. So you want to build muscle. But then you want to stoke that coal, and that's cardio. So, you need a balance of both things."

While resistance training builds muscle and strengthens bones and connective tissue, cardiovascular exercise challenges the heart and lungs, helping to maintain overall fitness, he said.

As adults age, Daikeler says the primary motivation for maintaining physical activity should shift away from aesthetic goals and toward functional mobility and independence.

Reflecting on his personal experience visiting his father in an assisted living facility, Daikeler observed how residents struggled with basic movement and balance.

Many residents relied on walkers and canes, and often stopped walking before talking to one another because they feared tripping over cracks in the pavement, he recalled.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"This is no longer about my abs," Daikeler added. "I need to work out in order to be able to walk and talk at the same time into my 90s ... It's no longer about aesthetics and vanity. It's really about mobility."

Maintaining healthy physical habits means accepting daily short-term discomfort to protect long-term independence, Daikeler noted.

"If I do 20 minutes of discomfort, the rest of the day is awesome," he said, adding that the goal is to consistently incorporate resistance training, cardio and flexibility work into a daily routine.

item.title: Trump launching 'Super Intelligence Force' to ensure American dominance
item.description: President Donald Trump said his new "Super Intelligence Force" will engage tech companies, religious groups and infrastructure providers to lead in superintelligence.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump announced Sunday the creation of a new federal "Super Intelligence Force" tasked with coordinating the government’s efforts to keep the United States at the forefront of rapidly developing artificial intelligence technology.

The new force, known as SIF, will coordinate federal engagement with consumers, public-interest and religious groups, critical infrastructure providers and technology companies, Trump said in a Truth Social post.

"The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence," Trump wrote.

TRUMP ANNOUNCES NEW 'AI FORCE,' VOWS TO PROTECT INDUSTRY AS AI CZAR ANNOUNCEMENT NEARS

Trump said the technology "is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet" and would "protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans."

The president said the effort will be led by senior administration officials and report directly to him and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

TRUMP REBRANDS AI, REJECTS 'GLOBALIST SCHEME' TO CONTROL TECH

Last week, Trump officially renamed artificial intelligence to "Super Intelligence" across the executive branch, following a high-level summit with top tech leaders at the White House.

Trump, who has opposed imposing formal guardrails on SI, said at the time that the tech executives signed a "morally binding" document he dubbed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

"They almost viewed it as a separate kind of constitution," Trump said of the tech leaders. "When they signed that, it meant a lot."

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X later that day that he viewed the summit as a "positive step."

"I think it's a significant positive step that the leaders of every major American lab have committed to implementing robust internal controls and multiple layers of audits and reviews," Zuckerberg wrote. 

Fox Business' Sophia Compton contributed to this report.

item.title: US Marine arrested in Japan over suspected killing of woman as Tokyo lodges 'strong protest'
item.description: Surveillance footage showed Anna Yagi entering a Naha hotel with Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard before he later left alone, police reported.
item.content:encoded:
A U.S. Marine stationed in Japan has been arrested on suspicion of robbing and killing a 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Okinawa, prompting Japanese officials to lodge a formal protest with the United States.

Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, is suspected of killing Anna Yagi at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa Prefecture, early Saturday and taking her wallet and backpack, according to Japanese police.

Ballard has denied the allegations, police said.

SERVICE MEMBER AMONG 2 ARRESTED AFTER MISSING MAN PROBE LEADS COPS TO BODY DUMP SITE ON ARMY BASE

Ballard is assigned to the III Marine Expeditionary Force and based at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, according to the Marine Corps.

Surveillance footage showed Yagi entering the hotel with Ballard before he later left alone, Stars and Stripes reported, citing Okinawa police. A hotel employee later found Yagi unresponsive after she failed to check out.

Police subsequently located Ballard in Okinawa City and arrested him, according to the outlet.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Okinawa Prefectural Police for additional information.

THAI RESORT CITY CRACKS DOWN ON PROSTITUTION AHEAD OF USS ABRAHAM LINCOLN ARRIVAL

The Marine Corps said it was cooperating with Japanese authorities and that Ballard remained in Japanese custody.

"The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behavior," the service said in a statement obtained by Reuters.

The arrest prompted swift condemnation from senior Japanese officials. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi offered condolences to Yagi's family and said her government had lodged a "strong protest" with the United States.

"The occurrence of such an extremely brutal and heinous incident is a matter of profound regret," Takaichi said in an English translation of her Japanese-language statement.

Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi also summoned U.S. Ambassador George Glass and called for full U.S. cooperation with the investigation, stricter discipline among American military personnel and measures to prevent similar incidents.

Glass expressed regret over the loss of life and pledged U.S. cooperation with Japanese authorities.

CHINA DEPLOYED OVER 100 VESSELS NEAR TAIWAN IN THE WAKE OF TRUMP-XI SUMMIT, TAIWAN SECURITY OFFICIAL CLAIMS

The case comes against a decades-long backdrop of tensions surrounding the large U.S. military presence in Okinawa.

Most of the roughly 18,000 Marines stationed in Japan are based on Okinawa, where crimes involving U.S. personnel, aircraft accidents and noise have periodically fueled local opposition to the American military presence.

Okinawa remains strategically important to the U.S.-Japan alliance because of its location in the western Pacific near Taiwan amid increased concern over China's military activity in the region.

Reuters contributed to this report.

item.title: GOP Senate candidate's estranged wife confirms who she's voting for amid divorce proceedings
item.description: Texas state Sen. Angela Paxton urges voters to back the GOP ticket without naming estranged husband Ken Paxton, who faces James Talarico in a tight Texas Senate race.
item.content:encoded:
Texas state Sen. Angela Paxton is addressing the "elephant in the room," saying she’ll vote Republican this November without mentioning one GOP candidate by name: her estranged husband, Ken Paxton.

Angela Paxton, who filed for divorce from the Texas Republican Senate candidate last year on "biblical grounds," says in a new political ad that she will back the Republican ticket on Nov. 3, arguing that keeping the seat in GOP hands outweighs concerns about any individual candidate.

"People have asked my thoughts about this election, and turns out, I have some," she says in the ad. "Let’s talk about the elephant in the room."

GOP FORTRESS IS UNDER THREAT IN ONE KEY RED STATE, AND THESE VOTERS COULD DECIDE WHETHER IT FALLS

"In a general election, it’s not as much about the individual players on the team; it’s about getting the whole team across the finish line," she continues. "Either we hold every Republican seat, or we hand the future of Texas to the other team."

"That’s why I’m voting for the Republican ticket on Nov. 3," she adds. "Let’s hold the line together."

The ad does not mention Ken Paxton by name, but its message comes as the Republican Senate candidate faces a tight general election contest against Democrat James Talarico.

The latest Fox News Poll, released Thursday, found Talarico with 51% support among Texas likely voters and Paxton with 49%, a difference within the poll’s margin of sampling error. The same poll found 50% of likely voters preferred Republican control of the U.S. Senate, compared with 49% who preferred Democratic control.

Angela Paxton has previously signaled that maintaining Republican control of the seat takes precedence over her feelings about the individual candidate.

item.title: ‘Addiction Economy’ is a bad gamble for young men. Here’s their way out
item.description: Roughly 35% of young men gamble daily or weekly as the 'Addiction Economy' exploits their isolation. But their ambitions reveal a path forward.
item.content:encoded:
You cannot scroll on social media, watch television or even make a purchase online without being inundated with advertisements for sports gambling and prediction markets. Companies are spending millions to make sure we see them, and their primary target audience is young men.

Data from the Institute for Family Studies confirms just how deeply this has taken hold: roughly one-third (35%) of young men gamble daily or weekly. This is not the only digital habit growing among young men today. Nearly half (42%) watch pornography daily or weekly, and most young men (86%) play video games daily or weekly.

This is what some people refer to as the "addiction economy." As a pastor, I know young men who engage in these things every day. And, to be honest, I’m not surprised. More than half (61%) of young men say they often feel they have little control over the things happening to them. Coping with this pervasive felt lack of agency drives them toward digital escapes that offer a temporary illusion of control, thrill or connection.

DAVID MARCUS: BRAVE NEW WORLD OF PREDICTION MARKETS CAN MAKE US ALL INSIDE TRADERS

Yet, we know two crucial things about today’s young men: they’re ambitious — and they’re vulnerable. An overwhelming majority (84%) of young men say they have ambitious plans for their future. They want to grow. They want to succeed, and in some sense feel that they’re capable of doing so.

But they’re also profoundly isolated and frustrated. They’re facing a world where the paths to traditional success — like career success, homeownership, marriage, children and more — feel washed away or blocked. They struggle with the ability to make friends with other young men or relate to young women.

AI IS CHANGING MODERN DATING, BUT EXPERTS WARN IT'S MAKING PEOPLE 'RELATIONALLY STUPID'

The addiction economy demands young men’s attention, time and money, and undermines their vision for a successful life. Left unchecked, society and commercial forces will continue to exploit or ignore their tendency at early ages to use things to numb pain, deal with anxiety, or cope with discouragement. But the true role of society should be to help them fulfill their aspirations for good and build lives of purpose.

If we don’t offer them a better vision for their lives, the addiction economy will gladly fill the void. Older generations are quick to notice and criticize young men for retreating into digital vices, but scolding and shaming have never produced excellence. Young men may be demoralized, but they haven’t given up. What they need is a guide and a path forward. They need to know they can build a life they actually want and can inhabit.

POLL FINDS SHARP RISE IN YOUNG MEN CALLING RELIGION 'VERY IMPORTANT'

Young men need formation and support if they are to develop their open-ended sense of potential and ambition into real success and healthy relationships with peers, colleagues and romantic partners. They are capable of building good and desirable lives for themselves, and of attaining real excellence. But they need help to do so. And any invested, stable adult is capable of providing the support they need. Their needs are ultimately simple, though urgent.

So, go out of your way to establish strong, authentic, transparent relationships with the young men in your life. Show them they’re not alone, that they’re not unique in their struggles. Provide relatability and accountability, hand in hand. These relationships will help remove the burden of guilt, of embarrassment, of shame for young men. This is part of being a human. We’re all going to struggle, often with the same things. These common struggles allow us to encourage and remind young men that they have the ability to overcome them.

DADS AREN’T OPTIONAL — AND AMERICA’S KIDS ARE PAYING THE BRUTAL PRICE

It’s also important to help young men feel like they have agency in their own lives, and that their lives have meaning. They have a lot of questions: how to be successful, find a fulfilling job, make friends and navigate dating. Often, we have to help them find answers and take practical steps to feel more in control of their future. Make sure they have the space they need to ask important questions and share vulnerable feelings or experiences, without feeling judged, dismissed or doubted.

Young men also need a clear vision for their lives, and a clear vision of how they fit into their own communities. Help them develop their ambitions into specific plans. Help them come to know and understand how much impact they can have, just by showing up to serve. Whether at work, at church, in their friendships or in their families, young men need opportunities to contribute, make a difference and see that their lives matter to the people around them.

I WORRY LESS ABOUT SCREENS THAN ABOUT THE CHALLENGES TODAY’S TEENS NEVER FACE

We as their mentors have to help them build lives they want to live. And in order to help them build those lives, we must step into their present lives without fear, without judgment and without hesitation. They want to succeed — they just need our support.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The addiction economy that has them firmly in its grasp isn’t something to be feared. It is one of the most profound opportunities for us to enter and help change the course of the lives of young men.

It’s time we stepped in.

item.title: GOP rising star helped topple Trump-backed incumbent. Now he's caught leadership's eye
item.description: Mike Haridopolos is emerging as a behind-the-scenes force on the East Coast, helping secure billions for NASA and Kennedy Space Center's future.
item.content:encoded:
It’s June 2026 and the summer’s intense heat is slowly creeping across the East Coast. In Florida, a different kind of heat is threatening to burn Republicans — a firestorm of political backlash that could at best force the GOP to spend millions more in the midterms, and at worst cost the party what should be a safely red House seat.

Rep. Mike Haridopolos, R-Fla., was one of the first to sound the alarm publicly about embattled Rep. Cory Mills, R-Fla., and the scandals that could have sandbagged his re-election chances. It’s an unusually bold move for a first-term congressman, particularly when all of the House GOP leadership and the White House were still publicly backing Mills.

But Haridopolos’ plan was well-executed — and with the help of Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., Mills went down as one of only four Republican incumbents to lose a primary in the 2026 midterm cycle. Republican election watchers saw the loss with some relief, privately feeling better about their chances with former journalist Ryan Elijah, who Haridopolos recruited to run, against Democratic former NASA official Bale Dalton.

And Haridopolos was there with Elijah both figuratively and literally. The former local news anchor said he was "right there in the front row" during the primary debate.

REPUBLICANS MOVE TO OUST EMBATTLED FLORIDA GOP LAWMAKER IN BITTER PRIMARY FIGHT

"Not only was he there, he was kind of like the spin room. He did a lot of the media interviews, and that was huge for us," Elijah told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP'S SUPPORT DOESN'T SAVE SCANDAL-PLAGUED LAWMAKER IN PRIMARY

Haridopolos told Fox News Digital, "I recognized that Cory Mills was absolutely going to lose a general election against a solid Democrat candidate. And so I went to the leadership and, of course, the president's team and said, look, we need to find a way for Mills to step aside."

"Unfortunately, Mr. Mills was not willing to step aside. And so I let the leadership and the president know that I'd be helping someone else in the primary," he continued. "It was not the easiest thing to do, taking on a colleague. But … this is a team sport and all of us need to work together."

WATCH: CORY MILLS BLASTS DOJ PROBE AS ‘POLITICAL OP' AHEAD OF FLORIDA PRIMARY

"Team sport" is an analogy that the Florida Republican has used frequently, and one that he’s used to try and define his tenure in the House.

It’s paid off for him so far, with Haridopolos having forged close relationships with both House GOP leaders and his peers.

"He’s a trusted ally and somebody you can count on. He delivers. You never have to worry about where he’s going to be," House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., who has known Haridopolos for roughly two decades, told Fox News Digital.

The two politicos first forged a relationship in their respective state houses. When Haridopolos said he would launch a campaign for Congress, Scalise said he told him, "I want to be your first check … I want to support you."

And in his short time so far, he's already been entrusted to lead a House panel. Haridopolos is chair of the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee’s space subcommittee, a fitting position for someone whose district is home to the Kennedy Space Center despite his junior status.

The Florida freshman said space has long been a passion of his, dating back to his efforts as a state lawmaker to bring the shuttle program back to his backyard.

NASA'S ARTEMIS FOLLOW-UP MISSION 'RIGHT AROUND THE CORNER' AFTER SUCCESSFUL LUNAR FLIGHT

"So many people were concerned that we'd go back to the post-Apollo days, which are very detrimental to the economy of Central Florida. And so at that time, Rick Scott was governor … We decided that we needed to not just rely on NASA but start pushing for public-private partnerships," Haridopolos said.

The U.S. has seen an unprecedented resurgence of success in space in the last two years, partly propelled by the public-private partnerships that Haridopolos is pushing. NASA completed its historic Artemis II mission just this year, sending four astronauts around the moon and back in the first such mission in decades.

PETER NAVARRO: TRUMP'S ARTEMIS VISION IS NOW FLYING — AND CHINA IS PAYING ATTENTION

"I'm really confident that in two years we'll be landing back on the moon," Haridopolos said.

That’s also due in no small part to the federal government investing in the new space race, after the Trump administration initially proposed a roughly 24% cut to NASA’s budget in May 2025.

Haridopolos, seeing space as another frontier for national security, was alarmed. He told Fox News Digital at the time that he would seek a "constructive conversation with the White House" about a higher figure.

"I’m not sure what that number will be in the end, but in my conversations with the president about space, he’s absolutely committed to it," he said in May 2025.

Eventually, President Donald Trump signed into law a spending bill that included $24.4 billion for NASA — rather than the initial $18.8 billion proposal — and approved an additional $9.9 billion in the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told Fox News Digital that Haridopolos "understands that so much of America’s future in space runs through Florida and Kennedy Space Center."

"He is serious about the mission, willing to engage on the hard issues, and always focused on how we can move the ball forward," Isaacman said.

Before his political career began, Haridopolos was a history professor at what is now Eastern Florida State College. He was born to an American mother and Greek immigrant father, and is currently married to Stephanie Haridopolos — a physician by profession who has spent the last several months as acting surgeon general.

But despite his accomplishments and connections, Haridopolos’ name is not one that has garnered headlines in the way that more bombastic House Republicans have in their public defiance of GOP leaders or criticism of Trump.

That’s because he prefers to settle disputes behind closed doors, a hallmark of politics that has largely been abandoned in an age where attention is seen as political currency.

"When you hear members of Congress saying, like, ‘Oh, I want you to get me on TV,’ it's usually like, ‘Uh-oh, someone’s about to do something crazy here to get on TV.’ He was like … I’m going to earn my spot on there legitimately by being a good, reliable messenger for the party," a Republican aide familiar with Haridopolos’ operation told Fox News Digital.

The aide said that could pose a challenge in times when television networks were looking for dramatic tales of discord, but that his communication skills still got him a "high volume" of press.

That aide said they also witnessed Haridopolos turn down media interviews that did not fit his schedule, but offer to help fellow House Republicans secure that spot instead.

"He was just finding ways to help out leadership, but also just his fellow members, especially his fellow freshman members," the aide said.

Haridopolos told Fox News Digital of the chaos that’s become a regular facet of Republicans' majority, "One of my goals is to tell those folks who always stand [in front of cameras] after we finish the session, you know, what we need to do more is spend time in the caucus having these knock-down, drag-outs. Not through the press, but as a family, and come out there unified. I think it's the best way to solve problems."

He’s also been known to offer help on the fundraising side — as Scalise put it, "He raises a lot of money."

The political maneuvering has raised questions for some about where Haridopolos sees his future and what he’s looking to get out of the relationships he is building in a largely transactional world.

"He knows how to work with people and how to advance what he wants," the Republican aide said. "I could see him in senior leadership … and sooner than people expect."

Scalise said, "Mike has a bright future, because he's a natural leader."

But Haridopolos has insisted that his efforts are all dedicated to the greater good of the Republican Party.

"A lot of people have asked me if I'm going to pursue a leadership position after the elections this year. I'm absolutely not going to pursue one of those leadership positions," he said. "There's people who have been in Congress for three, four, or five terms who I think have really put that effort in."

He named members like fellow freshman Rep. Brian Jack, R-Ga., Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas, and Rep. Rudy Yakym, R-Ind.

"If I'm focused on the team, I think great things could happen in the future," Haridopolos said.
